subtype: Approach: going back for a favourite toy [Pitfall]
passage: Note from Dolma, Tashi's mother. We practised the fire drill on Sunday evening. When I clapped the alarm signal, Tashi reached the landing on time, then turned and ran back inside for his budgie's cage. I caught him at the door. On the landing I told him: when the alarm sounds, things and even pets wait, and grown-ups take care of the rescue. My sister Madhuri added that a grown-up tells the firefighters if a pet is inside. Tashi cried a little, then asked, "Who will tell them about the budgie?" We said it is a grown-up's job. We will repeat the drill next Sunday. - Dolma

qa.q: What did Tashi run back inside for?
qa.a: Tashi ran back for his budgie's cage.

qa.q: What was Tashi feeling when he asked who will tell them about the budgie?
qa.a: Worried and upset about his pet, which is why he cried a little and asked.

qa.q: What could the family add to the plan so the budgie is not forgotten, and why?
qa.a: They could add a step where a grown-up names the pet to the firefighters, so Tashi knows someone is responsible.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Tashi's rush back inside?
qa.a: Dolma sees a loving but risky instinct, so she stops him at the door and uses it to teach.

grounding: In a practice drill a boy runs back for his pet's cage, and his parents teach that things and pets wait for adults.

passage:
Sunday
Diary, today we did our fire drill and I messed it up. Papa rang the steel plate like an alarm and shouted, "Fire! Out!" Jahnavi and Mummy went straight to the door. I ran the other way, to my room, to get Mitthu's cage. I could not leave Mitthu. Papa caught me at my door. He wasn't angry, but his face was serious. "In a real fire, those seconds can matter. People go out first. If Mitthu needs rescuing, the grown-ups or firefighters will do it." I cried a bit, because I love Mitthu. Then we did the drill again, and I went straight out. Papa hugged me at the gate. "That's my boy."
- Vijay

qa.q: What did Papa ring as the alarm?
How did Vijay feel when Papa explained the rule?
qa.a: Vijay felt sad and a bit upset, crying because of loving Mitthu, even though Papa was not angry.

qa.q: What else could the family plan for Mitthu, and why?
qa.a: They could decide that only an adult checks on pets, and keep the cage near the door, so no child turns back.

qa.q: How does the drill look to Jahnavi?
qa.a: Jahnavi goes straight to the door and may be surprised to see Vijay running the wrong way.

grounding: It shows a boy running back for his pet's cage during a practice drill, and his parents using it to teach that people get out first and adults lead any rescue.

passage: In their village house near Belgaum, Nitin's family practised a fire drill after a hut in the next lane caught fire. His mother, Usha, banged a pot. "Fire! Everyone out to the well!" Nitin was first up. But instead of running to the door, he darted back to the verandah for the parakeet's cage. Usha caught his arm. "Nitin, stop. What did we say?" "But the bird..." "In a real fire, you come out. If the bird can be saved, an adult will do it, or the fire brigade. You don't go back. Ever." Nitin's lip wobbled. They practised twice more, and both times he ran straight to the well, not looking back.

qa.q: Where was the family's meeting point?
How did Nitin feel when his mother stopped him?
qa.a: He felt upset and torn, worried about the parakeet, with his lip wobbling.

qa.q: What else could Usha do to help Nitin feel better about the rule?
qa.a: She could tell him which adult will check on the bird, so he trusts that someone is responsible for it.

qa.q: How does the drill look to Usha?
qa.a: Usha is alarmed to see Nitin run back, so she stops him and uses it to teach the rule clearly.

grounding: It shows a boy running back for his pet's cage in a practice drill, and his mother using it to teach that belongings and pets come second and adults lead rescue.
